clean_source_blocks.text: Mona Khalil, who had refused to leave the beach she had spent years protecting, died from her injuries after the Israeli strike.

Mona Khalil led decades-long effort to protect nesting site for turtles near her home in south of the country The Lebanese marine activist Mona Khalil, who became a beloved figure in the country for a decades-long effort to protect a nesting site for turtles near her home, has died from injuries sustained in an Israeli strike. Khalil, 76, ran a sanctuary called the Orange House Project near the Mediterranean city of Tyre. She hosted volunteers in her house to clean and monitor a mile-long beach and welcomed tourists to stay and learn about conservation. An Israeli airstrike hit her house earlier this month, severely wounding Khalil, who was moved to an intensive-care unit in Beirut before succumbing to her injuries on Friday, according to friends. Her assistant, an Ethiopian woman, suffered burns but was recovering.

Lebanese environmental activist Mona Khalil, whose work helped turn a stretch of coastline in southern Lebanon into one of the eastern Mediterranean's most important nesting sites for endangered sea turtles, has died after being wounded in an Israeli strike. Khalil, 76, was injured when her house on Mansouri beach, near the southern city of Tyre, was hit during Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon two weeks ago. She died on Friday after several days in hospital, according to a local environmental group. Her death came as Israeli air strikes intensified across southern Lebanon, raising concerns about renewed violence despite diplomatic efforts to maintain a fragile regional peace. The BBC has reached out to the Israeli military for a response. "She is a deeply committed environmental defender," Hisham Younes, the founder and president of Green Southerners, told the BBC.

"She used to talk about the beach like it was a person. Her bond to the sunset, her bond to the water and the turtles….she was really into conservation, and into the soul, the spirit of conservation." For more than 25 years, Khalil dedicated herself to protecting endangered loggerhead and green sea turtles that nest along Lebanon's southern coast. Her conservation work began after what her loved ones described as a life-changing encounter with a turtle laying eggs on Mansouri beach in 1999. A refugee of the Lebanese civil war, Khalil was living in the Netherlands but had returned to visit her family's seaside home. She was on the beach one night and saw a green turtle laying eggs on the beach.

Mona Khalil led decades-long effort to protect nesting site for turtles near her home in south of the country

The Lebanese marine activist Mona Khalil, who became a beloved figure in the country for a decades-long effort to protect a nesting site for turtles near her home, has died from injuries sustained in an Israeli strike.

Khalil, 76, ran a sanctuary called the Orange House Project near the Mediterranean city of Tyre. She hosted volunteers in her house to clean and monitor a mile-long beach and welcomed tourists to stay and learn about conservation.

An Israeli airstrike hit her house earlier this month, severely wounding Khalil, who was moved to an intensive-care unit in Beirut before succumbing to her injuries on Friday, according to friends. Her assistant, an Ethiopian woman, suffered burns but was recovering.

During the Lebanese civil war of 1975-90, Khalil moved to the Netherlands. She returned to her family’s land in 1999, where she had a chance encounter one evening with a turtle digging a nest in the sand on the beach.

Khalil painted the house orange to match the national colour of the Netherlands, which she said had given her refuge during a time of need, and started a protection and ecotourism project for loggerhead and green sea turtles that nest along Lebanon’s southern coast.

Foreign tourists had to coordinate their trip with the Lebanese military, as the bed and breakfast sat on land that Israel had repeatedly invaded and occupied. Those who managed to get permission would stay in Khalil’s idyllic home, with its flower-lined courtyard often filled with rescued dogs and cats. It is just a short walk through banana groves to the beach.

Regular power cuts and a lack of air-conditioning meant some visitors left unfavourable online reviews, although most were glowing as Khalil provided what other B&Bs could not – a chance to witness and help hatching turtles and to take part in protecting their vulnerable populations.

Khalil’s marine conservation efforts were initially resented by some local people, including property developers and fishers who used dynamite fishing, a practice she successfully fought against. Her house was also hit by Israeli bombardment during the 2006 war with Hezbollah.

payload.title: Libanonilainen merikilpikonnien suojelija Mona Khalil kuoli Israelin iskussa saamiinsa vammoihin
payload.summary: Mona Khalil, 76, tunnettiin Etelä-Libanonissa Mansourin rannan ja uhanalaisten merikilpikonnien pitkäaikaisena puolustajana. Hän kuoli sairaalassa haavoituttuaan Israelin iskussa kotitaloonsa Tyren lähellä.
payload.content:
Libanonilainen ympäristöaktivisti Mona Khalil on kuollut Israelin iskussa saamiinsa vammoihin. 76-vuotias Khalil oli omistanut yli 25 vuotta Mansourin rannan merikilpikonnien pesimäalueen suojelulle Etelä-Libanonissa Tyren kaupungin lähellä, eikä hän ollut halunnut jättää rantaa, jonka puolesta oli tehnyt työtä vuosikymmeniä.

## Pitkä työ uhanalaisten kilpikonnien hyväksi

Khalilin työ auttoi tekemään Etelä-Libanonin rannikkokaistaleesta yhden itäisen Välimeren tärkeistä pesimäalueista uhanalaisille merikilpikonnille. Hän suojeli erityisesti valekarettikilpikonnia ja liemikilpikonnia, jotka pesivät Libanonin etelärannikolla.

Khalil johti Orange House Project -nimistä suojelupaikkaa Mansourin rannalla. Hän majoitti vapaaehtoisia kotiinsa, jotta nämä voisivat puhdistaa ja valvoa noin mailin mittaista rantaa. Paikka otti vastaan myös matkailijoita, jotka halusivat oppia luonnonsuojelusta ja nähdä, miten pesimärantaa suojellaan.

Läheisten mukaan Khalilin elämäntyö alkoi vuonna 1999, kun hän näki vihreän merikilpikonnan munimassa Mansourin rannalla. Khalil oli Libanonin sisällissodan pakolainen ja asui tuolloin Alankomaissa, mutta oli palannut vierailulle perheensä merenrantakotiin. Kohtaamista kuvattiin hänen läheistensä mukaan elämää muuttaneeksi hetkeksi.

## Isku osui kotiin Mansourin rannalla

Khalil haavoittui vakavasti, kun hänen taloonsa osui Israelin ilmaisku Etelä-Libanonissa aiemmin tässä kuussa. Hänet siirrettiin tehohoitoon Beirutiin, missä hän kuoli perjantaina useiden sairaalapäivien jälkeen. Paikallisen ympäristöryhmän mukaan Khalilin kuolema seurasi kahden viikon takaista iskua Mansourin rannalla.

Khalilin etiopialainen avustaja sai palovammoja samassa iskussa, mutta hänen kerrottiin olevan toipumassa. BBC kertoi pyytäneensä Israelin armeijalta kommenttia iskuun.

## Huoli väkivallan kiihtymisestä

Khalilin kuolema tapahtui tilanteessa, jossa Israelin ilmaiskut Etelä-Libanonissa ovat voimistuneet. Se on lisännyt huolta väkivallan uudesta kiihtymisestä, vaikka alueella on pyritty pitämään yllä haurasta rauhaa diplomaattisin keinoin.

Green Southerners -järjestön perustaja ja puheenjohtaja Hisham Younes kuvasi Khalilia syvästi sitoutuneeksi ympäristön puolustajaksi. Läheiset ovat muistaneet häntä ihmisenä, joka puhui rannasta lähes kuin elävästä olennosta ja jonka suhde mereen, auringonlaskuihin ja kilpikonniin määritti hänen suojelutyötään.
summary_bullets: Mona Khalil kuoli Israelin iskussa saamiinsa vammoihin haavoituttuaan kotonaan Mansourin rannalla.
Khalil suojeli yli 25 vuoden ajan uhanalaisten merikilpikonnien pesimäaluetta Etelä-Libanonissa.
Hänen Orange House Project -suojelupaikkansa kokosi vapaaehtoisia puhdistamaan ja valvomaan rantaa Tyren lähellä.

The BBC has reached out to the Israeli military for a response. "She is a deeply committed environmental defender," Hisham Younes, the founder and president of Green Southerners, told the BBC.

"She used to talk about the beach like it was a person. Her bond to the sunset, her bond to the water and the turtles….she was really into conservation, and into the soul, the spirit of conservation." For more than 25 years, Khalil dedicated herself to protecting endangered loggerhead and green sea turtles that nest along Lebanon's southern coast. Her conservation work began after what her loved ones described as a life-changing encounter with a turtle laying eggs on Mansouri beach in 1999. A refugee of the Lebanese civil war, Khalil was living in the Netherlands but had returned to visit her family's seaside home. She was on the beach one night and saw a green turtle laying eggs on the beach.
